routine.content: Tell me about your typical day. What do you usually do from morning to night?

recent.content: Tell me about the last time you went to a restaurant. Where did you go, who were you with, and what did you eat?

compare.content: How have the ways people shop changed compared to the past? Compare shopping in the past and now.

anchors.text: Morning. I wake up. Seven. Eat bread. Um go school. Study. Home. Dinner. Sleep. Um. Every day same.

I wake up at seven o'clock. I eat breakfast with my mom. Then I go to school by bus. I have classes in the morning and afternoon. After school I go home. I eat dinner and watch TV. Sometimes I play games. I go to bed at twelve.

On weekdays I usually wake up at seven and I take a shower first. I don't eat breakfast because I don't have time, so I just drink some coffee. Then I take the subway to my university. It takes about forty minutes. I have classes until three or four. After class I go to the library and study, or sometimes I meet my friends and we eat something together. I get home around eight, and I have dinner and watch YouTube. I go to bed around one, so I'm always tired in the morning.

My typical day starts pretty early, around six thirty, because I have a part-time job at a cafe before my classes. I work there from seven to ten, so I make a lot of coffee for people who are going to work. After that I go to school, which is only ten minutes away. Most of my classes are in the afternoon, and I usually have two or three. Between classes I have lunch with my classmates at the student cafeteria, which is cheap but not that delicious. In the evening I go to the gym for about an hour because I'm trying to stay healthy. When I get home, I'm usually exhausted, so I just eat something simple and do my homework. I try to sleep before midnight, but honestly it doesn't happen very often.

So my weekdays are pretty packed, and I've kind of built a routine that keeps me sane. I'm up at six thirty, and the first thing I do is go for a short run along the stream near my apartment, because if I skip it, I feel sluggish for the rest of the day. After a quick shower I head to my part-time job at a cafe, where I work the morning rush from seven to ten. It's hectic, but I actually like it because the regulars know me and we chat a bit. Then I rush to campus for my afternoon classes. Lately I've been taking a statistics course that's really tough, so I usually stay in the library until about seven to review. When I finally get home, I cook something quick, like pasta or fried rice, and watch an episode of a drama to unwind. I used to stay up until two or three, but last semester my grades dropped, so now I'm trying to go to bed before midnight.

My weekdays follow a pretty tight rhythm, and over the past year I've realized that the routine itself is what keeps me from burning out. I'm up at six thirty, and before I even check my phone I go for a twenty-minute run along the stream behind my building. It sounds disciplined, but honestly it's the only part of the day that belongs entirely to me. From seven to ten I work the morning shift at a neighborhood cafe, which is chaotic in the best way. You get to know the regulars, like the nurse who always orders a double shot after her night shift, and those small conversations make the job feel less like work. Afternoons are for classes, and this semester they're mostly statistics and econometrics, so I usually end up in the library until seven going over problem sets. By the time I get home I'm drained, so I keep dinner simple and watch something light to switch off. I used to treat sleep as optional, but after my grades slipped last spring I started protecting it, and the difference in how I feel has been dramatic.
Restaurant. Last week. Friend. Um Korean food. Bulgogi. Good. Delicious. Um. Happy. Yes.

Last Saturday I went to a restaurant. I went with my friend. It was a Korean restaurant. We ate bulgogi and kimchi stew. The food was very delicious. The restaurant was clean. We talked a lot. It was a good day. I want to go there again.

The last time I went to a restaurant was last Saturday. I went to an Italian restaurant near my office with my coworker. It was her birthday, so we wanted to eat something special. We ordered a pasta with cream sauce and a pizza, and we also had some wine. The pasta was really good, but the pizza was a little bit salty. The restaurant was very crowded because it was the weekend, so we waited about twenty minutes. But the atmosphere was nice and we talked a lot. I think it was a good choice for her birthday.

The last time I ate out was last Saturday, when I went to a small Italian place near my office with my coworker Jiwon. It was actually her birthday, so I wanted to take her somewhere nicer than our usual lunch spots. When we got there, the place was packed, and we had to wait almost twenty minutes, which was a little annoying. But once we sat down, everything was great. We ordered a creamy mushroom pasta, a margherita pizza, and a glass of wine each. The pasta was amazing, but the pizza was a bit too salty for me. The best part was that the staff brought out a small cake with a candle because I had told them about her birthday when I made the reservation. She was really surprised and happy, so I felt proud of myself.

The last time I went out to eat was actually just last Saturday, and it turned into a pretty memorable evening. It was my coworker Jiwon's birthday, and since she'd been having a rough month at work, I wanted to take her somewhere a little special instead of our usual kimbap place. I found this tiny Italian restaurant tucked into an alley near our office, and I'd made a reservation, but when we showed up the place was so packed that we still ended up waiting about twenty minutes. I was kind of worried she'd be annoyed, but she said it gave us time to chat. Anyway, we ordered a creamy mushroom pasta and a margherita pizza to share. The pasta was honestly incredible, really rich but not heavy, while the pizza was a bit too salty. What made the night, though, was that when I booked I'd mentioned it was her birthday, and at the end the staff came out with a little tiramisu with a candle in it. She teared up a little, and I felt really glad I'd made the effort.

The last time I went out to eat was this past Saturday, and it ended up being one of those small evenings that stays with you. It was my coworker Jiwon's birthday, and she'd been having a brutal month, a project she'd poured herself into had just been shelved, so I wanted to take her somewhere that felt like a treat rather than our usual rushed lunch spots. I found a tiny Italian place tucked into an alley a few blocks from the office and booked a table, but even with the reservation we ended up waiting nearly twenty minutes because they'd overbooked. I was half expecting the night to go downhill from there, but she just laughed and said it was the first time in weeks she'd stood still long enough to talk. We shared a creamy porcini pasta, which was rich without being heavy, and a margherita pizza that, to be fair, was a little over-salted. The moment that made the night, though, came at the end. When I'd booked, I'd mentioned it was her birthday, and the staff quietly brought out a tiramisu with a single candle. She got a bit choked up, and walking back to the station she told me it was the first time in a while she'd felt someone had noticed her. That reminded me how much small gestures can matter.
Shopping. Before market. Now internet. Um phone. Fast. Easy. Before slow. Um. Now good.

In the past people went to the market. They bought things in stores. Now people shop on the internet. They use smartphones. It is very easy. Delivery is very fast. I like online shopping. But sometimes the clothes are not good. I think now is better.

Shopping has changed a lot compared to the past. In the past, people usually went to traditional markets or department stores to buy things. They could see the products and touch them before buying. But now most people shop online with their smartphones. It is very convenient because you can buy anything at home, and delivery is really fast in Korea. Sometimes you can get it the next morning. But there are some problems too. For example, sometimes the clothes look different from the pictures, so you have to return them. I think online shopping is more convenient, but I still go to stores sometimes.

I think shopping has changed a lot over the past ten or twenty years. When I was a kid, my mom used to take me to the traditional market every weekend. We would walk around, compare prices, and sometimes the sellers gave us extra vegetables for free. It took a long time, but it was kind of fun. Nowadays, most people, including me, do almost all their shopping on their phones. In Korea, delivery is so fast that if you order before midnight, you can get it the next morning. It's really convenient, especially for busy people. However, I think something is missing. You can't talk with the sellers anymore, and it's easy to spend too much money because buying things is just one click. So even though online shopping is more convenient, I sometimes miss the old way.

Shopping has changed so much that it almost feels like a different activity compared to when I was growing up. Back then, shopping was kind of a social event. My mom would take me to the traditional market on weekends, and she'd spend ages comparing prices and chatting with the vendors, who usually threw in some extra green onions or something because they knew us. Department stores were for special occasions, like buying a winter coat. These days, though, almost everything happens on our phones. In Korea especially, with next-morning delivery, you can order groceries at eleven at night and have them at your door before breakfast, which honestly still amazes me. The upside is obvious, it saves a ton of time. But I think we've lost something too. Shopping used to involve actual people, and now it's just scrolling and clicking, and I've noticed that I buy way more stuff I don't really need. So I'd say it's more efficient now, but not necessarily better.

I'd say shopping has shifted from being a social activity to something closer to a background task, and that shift has happened remarkably quickly. When I was a kid, going shopping meant a trip to the traditional market with my mom. It could easily take a whole morning, because she'd move from stall to stall comparing prices and chatting with vendors who knew our family, and more often than not someone would slip an extra handful of green onions into our bag. Department stores were reserved for bigger purchases, like a winter coat or a gift. Today the entire process has collapsed into a few taps on a phone. Korea's logistics have become so efficient that you can order groceries just before midnight and find them at your door before you've had breakfast. That convenience is genuinely transformative, especially for people working long hours. At the same time, I think we've traded away more than we realize. The friction that used to slow us down, walking, comparing, talking to an actual person, also acted as a kind of filter, and without it it's frighteningly easy to buy things on impulse. So while shopping is undeniably more efficient now, I'm not convinced it's better, and I find myself deliberately going to the market now and then just to keep that older rhythm alive.
